title: A Sleeping Mother Nature Wins Top Prize at Chelsea Flower Show
summary:
At this year's RHS Chelsea Flower Show, a giant sleeping figure of Gaia—the ancient Greek goddess of the Earth—has taken the top prize. The garden, titled 'On the Edge,' was designed by Sarah Eberle in collaboration with the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE). It celebrates 'edgelands,' the often-overlooked spaces between rural and urban areas, like roadside berms and canal banks.

The centerpiece is a massive reclining figure of Gaia, with willow-branch locks crafted by artist Tom Hare and a crown of leaves. Her face and shoulders are carved from a fallen mature tree by Tim Wood. A winding path leads under an arch that forms her torso, built in the tradition of dry stone walls by Noble Stonework. The garden uses native plants with a wild, untamed aesthetic, encouraging visitors to see beauty in what might be dismissed as weeds.

CPRE says these edgelands 'connect millions of people to nature in everyday life, yet they're undervalued and under constant pressure.' The garden aims to change that perspective. Eberle describes the effect as 'a sense of abundance, a landscape under repair, the beauty in the ordinary. It's about how it makes you feel—it's almost a homecoming, an embrace, a hug.'

The Chelsea Flower Show, hosted by the Royal Horticultural Society, has been held since 1913. This year's show runs through May 23 in London. If you're lucky enough to visit, you can see Gaia snoozing peacefully amid a riot of native plants—a gentle reminder to appreciate the wild edges of our world.
why_it_matters: The garden challenges us to find beauty in forgotten places, teaching that even the scraggly roadside weeds are worth protecting—a lesson important for future environmental stewards. Recognizing the value of these spaces can help preserve biodiversity where we live.

background_read: The Chelsea Flower Show, hosted by the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS, a UK gardening charity founded in 1804), has been a major event since 1913, showcasing cutting-edge garden design.
The winning garden was made in partnership with the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE, a charity that has fought for countryside preservation since 1926).

The garden highlights 'edgelands,' those overlooked border zones—roadside verges, canal banks, railway embankments—that are often rich in wild plants and animals but face constant pressure from building projects.
The figure of Gaia comes from ancient Greek mythology, where she is the primordial Earth mother; in modern environmental thinking, Gaia also represents the idea of Earth as a single living organism.

perspectives.description: The garden encourages people to value overlooked spaces and could inspire more wildlife-friendly gardening, boosting biodiversity in cities and suburbs. It also shows that beauty doesn't have to be expensive or manicured.

Some traditional garden enthusiasts might argue that messy 'edgelands' don't fit the formal beauty standards of a prestigious flower show, potentially devaluing traditional horticulture. There's a risk that 'wild' gardening might be seen as an excuse for neglect.

The design reflects a growing trend in landscape architecture to embrace ecological function over manicured perfection, acknowledging that human management often reduces habitat for insects and birds. It's part of a wider movement to rethink how we use urban space.

If the concept catches on, future urban planning might intentionally protect edgelands as green corridors, connecting people to nature and helping species migrate in a changing climate. This could lead to policies that reward communities for keeping wild areas intact.
